cards.front: What does a single point represent on a scatter graph?
cards.back: A pair of data (two pieces of information) for the same object or event.

options.text: A pair of data (two pieces of information) for the same object or event.
options.explanation: Each point combines the values of the two variables for one object or event, with one coordinate read from each axis.

options.text: A single value (one piece of information) for the same object or event.
options.explanation: Treating a point as one value ignores its second coordinate. Each point represents a pair of data values for the same object or event.

options.text: A pair of data (two pieces of information) from two different objects or events.
options.explanation: The two coordinates must describe the same object or event, not two different ones. Together, they form one paired data point.

options.text: An average value (a summary of information) for the whole data set.
options.explanation: A point records an individual pair of values rather than an average of the data set. Each coordinate gives one variable for the same case.

cards.front: How do variables change in positive correlation?
cards.back: As one variable increases, the other variable tends to increase.

options.text: As one variable increases, the other variable tends to increase.
options.explanation: Positive correlation means that higher values of one variable are generally associated with higher values of the other, although individual points may not follow the trend exactly.

options.text: As one variable increases, the other variable tends to decrease.
options.explanation: This describes negative correlation, where the variables generally move in opposite directions. In positive correlation, the other variable tends to increase.

options.text: As one variable increases, the other variable tends to stay constant.
options.explanation: A variable staying constant would not create an upward trend. Positive correlation occurs when the other variable generally increases as the first increases.

options.text: As one variable increases, the other variable changes with no pattern.
options.explanation: Random change with no overall pattern indicates no correlation. Positive correlation produces a general upward trend from left to right.

cards.front: How do variables change in negative correlation?
cards.back: As one variable increases, the other variable tends to decrease.

options.text: As one variable increases, the other variable tends to decrease.
options.explanation: Negative correlation means that higher values of one variable are generally associated with lower values of the other, producing a downward trend from left to right.

options.text: As one variable increases, the other variable tends to increase.
options.explanation: This is positive correlation because both variables generally move in the same direction. In negative correlation, the other variable tends to decrease.

options.text: As one variable increases, the other variable tends to stay constant.
options.explanation: A constant second variable would not produce the downward trend required for negative correlation. The other variable should generally decrease as the first increases.

options.text: As one variable increases, the other variable changes with no pattern.
options.explanation: An absence of any pattern indicates no correlation. Negative correlation has a recognisable downward trend because one variable tends to decrease as the other increases.

cards.front: To identify the type of correlation, you should look at the overall direction of the points from [ ___ ].
cards.back: To identify the type of correlation, you should look at the overall direction of the points from left to right.

options.text: left to right
options.explanation: Scatter graphs are conventionally read from left to right. An upward overall direction indicates positive correlation, while a downward direction indicates negative correlation.

options.text: top to bottom
options.explanation: Correlation is classified by following the points horizontally from left to right, not vertically from top to bottom. This reveals whether the overall trend rises or falls.

options.text: centre outwards
options.explanation: Looking from the centre outwards does not give the standard direction needed to classify the trend. Follow the points from left to right instead.

options.text: point to point
options.explanation: Following individual points encourages joining the dots and misses the overall pattern. Correlation is identified from the general direction of the points from left to right.

cards.front: Does correlation between two variables prove that one causes the other?
cards.back: No.It shows they are linked in the data, but not causation.

options.text: No.It shows they are linked in the data, but not causation.
options.explanation: Correlation identifies an association between variables, but another variable or coincidence may explain it. Therefore, correlation alone cannot establish that one variable causes the other.

options.text: Yes.It shows one variable is responsible for the change in the other.
options.explanation: This confuses association with causation. A correlation shows that variables are linked in the data, but it does not prove that either variable causes the other.

options.text: Yes.It proves the variables have a cause-and-effect relationship.
options.explanation: Even a strong correlation cannot prove a cause-and-effect relationship because other factors may affect both variables. It establishes a link in the data only.

options.text: No.It shows the variables are unrelated and have no connection.
options.explanation: Saying there is no connection ignores the observed correlation. The variables are linked in the data, but that link alone does not demonstrate causation.

cards.front: If points are spread randomly with no clear direction, the graph shows [ ___ ].
cards.back: If points are spread randomly with no clear direction, the graph shows no correlation.

options.text: no correlation
options.explanation: No correlation occurs when the points have no recognisable upward or downward trend and appear randomly spread across the scatter graph.

options.text: positive correlation
options.explanation: Positive correlation requires a general upward trend from left to right. Randomly spread points with no clear direction show no correlation.

options.text: negative correlation
options.explanation: Negative correlation requires a general downward trend from left to right. If the points have no clear direction, there is no correlation.

options.text: perfect correlation
options.explanation: Perfect correlation would place all points exactly on a straight line. A random spread with no overall direction instead indicates no correlation.

cards.front: State two rules for drawing a sensible line of best fit.
cards.back: Follow the overall trend/direction of the points.Keep roughly the same number of points on each side of the line.

options.text: Follow the overall trend/direction of the points.Keep roughly the same number of points on each side of the line.
options.explanation: A sensible line of best fit represents the overall pattern rather than individual points. Balancing the points approximately evenly on either side helps prevent bias.

options.text: Join every point in the order plotted.Make sure the line passes through all of the points.
options.explanation: Joining every point creates a line graph rather than a line of best fit, and scattered data rarely lie on one line. The line should follow the overall trend.

options.text: Follow the steepest possible direction through the points.Keep roughly all of the points below the line.
options.explanation: Choosing the steepest line and placing all points below it biases the result. The line should follow the overall trend with roughly equal numbers on each side.

options.text: Draw from the origin to the furthest point on the graph.Make sure the line passes through the origin.
options.explanation: A line of best fit need not pass through the origin or the furthest point. Its position should be determined by the overall distribution of all points.

cards.front: Why is it incorrect to "join the dots" on a scatter graph?
cards.back: A scatter graph is not a line graph; you must use a single straight line of best fit to show the trend.

options.text: A scatter graph is not a line graph; you must use a single straight line of best fit to show the trend.
options.explanation: The points are separate paired observations and have no required sequence for joining. A single line of best fit summarises their overall trend.

options.text: A scatter graph is a line graph; you must connect consecutive points with straight line segments to show the trend.
options.explanation: This confuses scatter graphs with line graphs. Scatter points are not consecutive values to be joined; one straight line of best fit should represent the trend.

options.text: A scatter graph is not a line graph; you must draw a smooth curve through every point to show the trend.
options.explanation: A curve through every point overfits individual observations rather than summarising the relationship. At GCSE, a single straight line of best fit is used to show the trend.

options.text: A scatter graph is a coordinate grid; you must join each point to the origin of the axes to show the trend.
options.explanation: Lines from each point to the origin do not represent correlation and have no role in a scatter graph. The overall trend is shown with one line of best fit.

cards.front: Must the line of best fit always pass through the origin $(0,0)$?
cards.back: No, only if the points suggest it should.

options.text: No, only if the points suggest it should.
options.explanation: A line of best fit should follow the pattern of the plotted points. It passes through $(0,0)$ only when the observed trend makes the origin appropriate.

options.text: Yes, whenever both of the axes start at zero.
options.explanation: Starting both axes at zero does not force the data trend through the origin. The correct answer is no; the line passes through $(0,0)$ only if the points suggest it should.

options.text: Yes, every line of best fit must pass through the origin.
options.explanation: A line of best fit represents the data trend rather than following a fixed rule about the origin. It need not pass through $(0,0)$ unless the points support this.

options.text: No, a line of best fit should never pass through the origin.
options.explanation: Avoiding the origin automatically is just as mistaken as always using it. A line of best fit may pass through $(0,0)$ when that matches the pattern of points.

cards.front: How is a line of best fit used to estimate a $y$-value from a given $x$-value?
cards.back: Start at the $x$-value on the horizontal axis and move up to the line.Move across to the vertical axis to read the value.

options.text: Start at the $x$-value on the horizontal axis and move up to the line.Move across to the vertical axis to read the value.
options.explanation: Moving vertically from the given $x$-value locates the corresponding point on the line of best fit. Moving horizontally to the vertical axis then gives the estimated $y$-value.

options.text: Start at the $x$-value on the horizontal axis and move across to the line.Move up to the horizontal axis to read the value.
options.explanation: Moving across from the horizontal axis changes the $x$-coordinate instead of keeping the given one fixed. Move up to the line first, then across to the vertical axis.

options.text: Start at a $y$-value on the vertical axis and move across to the line.Move down to the horizontal axis to read the value.
options.explanation: The method must begin with the given $x$-value, not a chosen $y$-value. Move up from the horizontal axis to the line, then across to the vertical axis.

options.text: Start at the $x$-value on the horizontal axis and move up to the nearest point.Move across to the vertical axis to read the value.
options.explanation: Using the nearest plotted point ignores the line of best fit and may give an unrepresentative estimate. Move up to the line itself, then across to the vertical axis.

cards.front: What is the exam benefit of drawing construction lines when estimating?
cards.back: They make the method clear even if the final estimate is slightly off.

options.text: They make the method clear even if the final estimate is slightly off.
options.explanation: Construction lines show how the value was obtained from the axes and line of best fit. This can demonstrate a correct method despite a small reading or drawing error.

options.text: They guarantee the estimate is exact even if the line of best fit is slightly off.
options.explanation: Construction lines record the reading process but cannot make an estimate exact. Their benefit is showing a clear method, which may earn credit despite a slightly inaccurate final value.

options.text: They make the graph more accurate even if some of the plotted points are slightly off.
options.explanation: Construction lines do not alter the plotted data or improve the graph’s underlying accuracy. They show the method used to obtain an estimate from the line of best fit.

options.text: They remove the need for a line of best fit when the final estimate is slightly off.
options.explanation: Construction lines are used alongside, not instead of, a line of best fit. Their exam benefit is making the estimation method clear when the final reading is slightly inaccurate.

cards.front: [ ___ ] means estimating within the range of the data, while extrapolation means estimating outside the range.
cards.back: Interpolation means estimating within the range of the data, while extrapolation means estimating outside the range.

options.text: Interpolation
options.explanation: Interpolation is the process of estimating a value between known values and within the observed data range, where the existing trend is supported by plotted evidence.

options.text: Extrapolation
options.explanation: Extrapolation means estimating beyond the observed data range, not within it. The required term is interpolation because the estimate lies inside the range of known data.

options.text: Correlation
options.explanation: Correlation describes the strength and direction of a relationship between two variables; it is not an estimation method. Estimating within the data range is called interpolation.

options.text: Causation
options.explanation: Causation means that one variable directly produces a change in another, rather than estimating a value from a graph. The correct term for estimation within the range is interpolation.

cards.front: Interpolation means estimating within the range of the data, while [ ___ ] means estimating outside the range.
cards.back: Interpolation means estimating within the range of the data, while extrapolation means estimating outside the range.

options.text: extrapolation
options.explanation: Extrapolation estimates values beyond the smallest or largest observed data values. Such predictions are less reliable because the existing trend might not continue outside the plotted range.

options.text: interpolation
options.explanation: Interpolation estimates within the observed data range, which is the opposite of the definition required here. Estimating beyond the range of plotted data is called extrapolation.

options.text: correlation
options.explanation: Correlation describes how two variables are associated and does not mean making an estimate outside the data range. The correct term for such an estimate is extrapolation.

options.text: causation
options.explanation: Causation is a direct cause-and-effect relationship, not a type of graphical estimation. An estimate made outside the observed range of data is called extrapolation.

cards.front: Why is extrapolation considered unreliable?
cards.back: There is no guarantee the trend will continue beyond the plotted data.

options.text: There is no guarantee the trend will continue beyond the plotted data.
options.explanation: Extrapolation assumes that the observed relationship continues into an area where there are no plotted points to support it. The pattern may change beyond the recorded range.

options.text: The line of best fit ends at the final plotted point in the data.
options.explanation: A line of best fit can be extended beyond the final point, so its graphical endpoint is not the problem. Extrapolation is unreliable because the trend itself may not continue.

options.text: All values beyond the plotted range are impossible for the given data.
options.explanation: Values outside the observed range are not necessarily impossible; they are simply unsupported by the available evidence. Extrapolation is unreliable because the existing trend might not continue.

options.text: Not every point lies exactly on the line within the plotted data.
options.explanation: Scatter graphs rarely have every point exactly on the line, but that is not the specific problem with extrapolation. Its unreliability comes from assuming the trend continues beyond the evidence.

cards.front: Estimating within the data range is [ ___ ] than estimating outside of it.
cards.back: Estimating within the data range is more reliable than estimating outside of it.

options.text: more reliable
options.explanation: Interpolation uses a trend within the region supported by observed data points. Extrapolation extends the trend beyond that evidence, so estimating within the range is generally more reliable.

options.text: less reliable
options.explanation: This reverses the reliability relationship. Estimates within the data range are more reliable because nearby plotted points support the trend, whereas values beyond the range depend on an unsupported continuation.

options.text: equally reliable
options.explanation: The two methods are not generally equally dependable. Interpolation is more reliable because it estimates among observed data, while extrapolation assumes the trend continues into an unobserved region.

options.text: more uncertain
options.explanation: This wrongly suggests that estimates supported by surrounding data involve greater uncertainty. Estimating within the range is more reliable because the plotted evidence supports the local trend.

cards.front: Can you use a line of best fit if the graph shows no correlation?
cards.back: No, it will not provide a meaningful or useful estimate.

options.text: No, it will not provide a meaningful or useful estimate.
options.explanation: With no correlation, changes in $x$ do not give a consistent indication of $y$. Any fitted line would therefore produce estimates unsupported by a meaningful pattern.

options.text: Yes, drawing it through the centre will provide a useful estimate.
options.explanation: A central line does not represent a predictive relationship when the points show no correlation. The correct answer is no because such a line cannot provide a meaningful estimate.

options.text: Yes, having enough plotted points will make the estimate meaningful.
options.explanation: A large number of points cannot create a relationship when the scatter still shows no correlation. A line of best fit is not useful because $x$ does not meaningfully predict $y$.

options.text: Yes, provided that both axes begin at zero on the graph.
options.explanation: Starting the axes at zero affects how the graph is displayed, not whether the variables are correlated. With no correlation, a line of best fit cannot produce useful estimates.

cards.front: In a scatter graph context, what defines the range of the data?
cards.back: From the smallest plotted value to the largest plotted value on an axis.

options.text: From the smallest plotted value to the largest plotted value on an axis.
options.explanation: The range covered by plotted data extends from the lowest observed value to the highest observed value on the relevant axis.

options.text: From zero to the largest numbered value shown on an axis.
options.explanation: Starting at zero confuses the data range with the full axis scale. The data range runs from the smallest plotted value to the largest plotted value.

options.text: From the first plotted value to the last plotted value on an axis.
options.explanation: Plotting order does not determine the range. The relevant endpoints are the smallest and largest plotted values, regardless of which points were plotted first or last.

options.text: From the smallest axis label to the largest axis label shown on an axis.
options.explanation: This describes the displayed axis scale rather than the data range. The range of the data extends from the smallest plotted value to the largest plotted value.

cards.front: When plotting a point with coordinates $(12, 30)$, you move [ ___ ] along the horizontal axis and 30 up the vertical axis.
cards.back: When plotting a point with coordinates $(12, 30)$, you move 12 along the horizontal axis and 30 up the vertical axis.

options.explanation: Coordinates are written in the order $(x, y)$, so the first coordinate gives the horizontal movement. Therefore, $(12, 30)$ requires moving 12 along the horizontal axis.
This swaps the two coordinates, a common plotting error. In $(12, 30)$, the first coordinate is horizontal, so the required horizontal movement is 12.
Subtracting the coordinates does not determine either position on a scatter graph. The first coordinate directly gives the horizontal movement, which is 12.
Adding the two coordinates does not give the horizontal position. Coordinates are read separately, and the first coordinate shows that the point moves 12 horizontally.

cards.front: When plotting a point with coordinates $(12, 30)$, you move 12 along the horizontal axis and [ ___ ] up the vertical axis.
cards.back: When plotting a point with coordinates $(12, 30)$, you move 12 along the horizontal axis and 30 up the vertical axis.

options.explanation: Coordinates are written in the order $(x, y)$, so the second coordinate gives the vertical movement. Therefore, $(12, 30)$ requires moving 30 up the vertical axis.
This swaps the horizontal and vertical coordinates. In $(12, 30)$, the second coordinate controls the vertical position, so the point moves 30 up.
Subtracting the first coordinate from the second does not give the vertical position. The second coordinate directly states the vertical movement, which is 30.
Adding the coordinates is not part of plotting an ordered pair. The vertical position is given directly by the second coordinate, so it is 30.

cards.front: What determines whether a variable is placed on the horizontal or vertical axis?
cards.back: The labels provided in the question or table (e.g., hours revised on horizontal).

options.text: The labels provided in the question or table (e.g., hours revised on horizontal).
options.explanation: Axis labels identify which variable belongs on each axis. The question, table or partially labelled graph indicates the intended placement, such as hours revised on the horizontal axis.

options.text: The size of each variable’s values (e.g., larger values on horizontal).
options.explanation: Variables are not assigned to axes according to numerical size. Their placement is determined by the labels or instructions provided in the question or table.

options.text: The order of the collected results (e.g., first result on horizontal).
options.explanation: The order in which results were collected does not assign variables to axes. The labels in the question or table show which variable belongs on each axis.

options.text: The units used for each variable (e.g., hours always on horizontal).
options.explanation: No unit is permanently linked to one axis, so hours need not always be horizontal. The supplied labels or instructions determine the placement of each variable.

cards.front: A variable is something that [ ___ ], such as height or price.
cards.back: A variable is something that can change, such as height or price.

options.text: can change
options.explanation: A variable is a quantity or characteristic whose value can differ between observations, people or situations, such as height, price or time.

options.text: stays fixed
options.explanation: A quantity that stays fixed is a constant, not a variable. A variable can change or take different values, such as height or price.

options.text: has no value
options.explanation: Variables do have values, although those values may differ between observations. The defining feature is that a variable can change, not that it lacks a value.

options.text: must increase
options.explanation: A variable may increase, decrease or remain unchanged between particular observations. It is called a variable because it can change, not because it must increase.

cards.front: What are the three main types of correlation?
cards.back: Positive correlationNegative correlationNo correlation

options.text: Positive correlationNegative correlationNo correlation
options.explanation: Scatter graphs are classified by whether both variables tend to increase together, one tends to decrease as the other increases, or there is no evident relationship.

options.text: Strong correlationWeak correlationNo correlation
options.explanation: Strong and weak describe the strength of a relationship, not its main directional type. The three main types are positive, negative and no correlation.

options.text: Direct correlationInverse correlationEqual correlation
options.explanation: These terms confuse correlation with proportional relationships, and equal correlation is not a standard type. Scatter graphs use positive, negative and no correlation.

options.text: Linear correlationCurved correlationRandom correlation
options.explanation: Linear and curved describe the shape of a pattern rather than the three main correlation types. Those types are positive, negative and no correlation.
